text: You're given an integer array called nums. You start at index zero. Each value, nums at i, is the maximum jump length from index i. Return true if you can reach the last index, and false otherwise.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — from index i, I can jump any distance from one up to nums at i, not only exactly that value. I only jump forward. And I just need a yes or no. I don't need the number of jumps, or the actual path. Is that right?
Yes. Any length up to the max, forward only, and just true or false.

Okay. Then there's one fact I want to say early. If I can reach some index j, I can reach every index before j too, because the jump that lands on j could just stop shorter. So the set of reachable indices is always a prefix, from zero up to some farthest point. That means I don't need to track a whole set. One number is enough: how far the prefix goes. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The length is between one and ten to the fourth, and every value is between zero and ten to the fifth.

Got it. So n is at least one. With one element, I'm already standing on the last index, so the answer is true. Values can be zero, and zeros are the only thing that can block me. And the biggest sum I'll compute is i plus nums at i, at most nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine plus one hundred thousand. That's tiny for a regular int. Let me run through the examples. First: two, three, one, one, four. From index zero I can reach index one or two. From index one I can jump three, straight to index four, the last one. So that's true. Now: three, two, one, zero, four. From index zero, one, two, or three, the farthest I can get is index three, every single time. And index three holds a zero, so it's a wall. I can never get past it to index four. So that's false.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to treat it as a graph. Each index has edges to the next few indices it can jump to. Then I run a breadth-first search, or a dynamic program where reach of j is true if some earlier reachable index can jump to j or beyond. That's correct, and I'd keep it as a checker. But it touches every edge, so it can be quadratic. With ten thousand elements and jumps up to a hundred thousand, that's wasted work. This problem reminds me of a greedy frontier scan — a running-maximum sweep over one growing covered interval, the same exchange idea as merging overlapping intervals into a single covered prefix. Because the reachable set is a prefix, I only need to push its right edge forward. Each index that's inside the prefix offers a new edge, i plus nums at i. I take the max. One pass, no set, no queue.

Here's the plan. I keep one variable, farthest — the farthest index reachable using only the indices before the current one. The invariant is that the reachable set is exactly zero up to farthest. I start it at zero. Then, for each index i from left to right: first, if i is greater than farthest, i is outside the prefix, so I return false. Otherwise, I update farthest to the max of itself and i plus nums at i. If the loop finishes, every index, including the last one, was reachable, so I return true. Here, I'm using farthest to keep track of the right edge of the reachable prefix. When I arrive at index i, farthest only counts jumps from earlier indices. If i is beyond farthest, nobody before i can reach i. And since the set is a prefix, nothing after i is reachable either. So I can stop and return false right there. One thing worth flagging — the order of the two lines matters. The check must come before the update. Let me walk through that. If I update first, then farthest is at least i plus nums at i, which is at least i. So the check can never fire. The function never returns false. It fails every unreachable case, including example two, and even a tiny array of two zeros. There's a trade-off here. I could also go backward. Keep a goal, starting at the last index, and walk from the end to the front. If i plus nums at i reaches the goal, then i can reach the goal, so I move the goal down to i. At the end, return whether the goal is zero. That's also linear time and constant space, and it's correct. But the forward version can stop early at the first wall, and it says the prefix idea directly. So I'll go forward. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I'll think out loud as I go. I write a function canJump that takes the array. I read the size into n, and I start farthest at zero. Then I loop i from zero up to n minus one. Inside the loop, first the check: if i is greater than farthest, I return false. Then the update: farthest becomes the max of farthest and i plus nums at i. After the loop, I return true. That matches the plan line by line. One thing worth flagging — the compare is strictly greater, not greater or equal. When i equals farthest, i is the last reachable index. That's fine, I'm standing on it. If I wrote greater or equal, then at i equals zero the check would be zero greater or equal to zero, which is true. So it would return false on the very first step, for every input. Even the single-element array with one zero, where the answer is true. And the max is needed. It's tempting to just assign farthest equals i plus nums at i, but a small value later would pull the edge back. Take two, zero, zero. Index zero sets farthest to two. Then index one would set it back to one plus zero, which is one, and index two looks unreachable. That returns false, but the answer is true. The sneaky part: that version passes both official examples.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. I'll use example two — three, two, one, zero, four — because it's the false case. Expected output is false. At index zero, farthest starts at zero. The check passes, and zero plus three pushes farthest to three. Then indices one, two, and three all offer exactly three again: one plus two, two plus one, three plus zero. So farthest is stuck at three. The turning point is i equals four. The check asks: is four greater than three? Yes. So I return false, right there. The zero at index three is the wall, and the four at index four never gets used — and that's right, because I can never stand there. Quickly, example one: two, three, one, one, four. Farthest goes to two, then to four at index one, then stays at four. At i equals four, four is not greater than four, so I'm on the last index. The loop ends after five steps, and I return true. That matches. Let's also test with corner cases. A single zero gives true — the check passes once, the loop ends, and I'm already at the last index. Zero then one gives false — stuck at index zero. Two, zero, zero gives true — farthest stays at two and reaches the end exactly; this is the case that breaks the no-max version. One, zero, one, zero gives false — farthest is one, and the one at index two doesn't help, because I never reach it. Ten thousand zeros: false after just two iterations. All ones: true, with farthest ending at ten thousand. And one huge first jump followed by zeros: true — index zero covers everything in one go.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is linear. One pass, and each step is one compare and one max. The space complexity is constant. Just two integers. In the worst-case scenario I go through all n indices. For a true answer that's always n steps. The worst false case is all ones with a zero just before the end — then the wall is found only at the very last index, after all ten thousand iterations. The full-size array runs all ten thousand steps in about eight microseconds. And the biggest value farthest can ever hold is about one hundred ten thousand. Int max is about two point one billion, so a plain int is safe. No long long needed. Oh, one more thing — I'd test this against the breadth-first-search checker. I ran every array of length one to eight with values zero to three. That's about eighty-seven thousand arrays — forty-one thousand six hundred true, and forty-five thousand seven hundred eighty false. Plus random large ones, for over three hundred thousand cases total, with zero mismatches. The same test shows how the small bugs fail. Update-before-check fails exactly the false arrays. Greater-or-equal fails exactly the true arrays. And dropping the max fails about twenty-eight thousand cases, while still passing both official examples. The backward-goal version had zero fails too.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw early that the reachable set is always a prefix, so one number, farthest, replaces the whole breadth-first search. You explained why the check must come before the update, and why it's strictly greater and not greater or equal — one bug never says false, the other always does. And you showed the max is a correctness need, with two, zero, zero — a case both official examples miss. Good work.
